title: Logo Exploration: AI as Sketchbook, Not Final Art

production_notes: [VERIFY] Copyright protection for AI-assisted logos is unsettled. The script states only the principle that copyright rules for mostly AI-made work are unclear and differ by country; it leaves out content.md's claim that some authorities have said such works may not be protected. Redrawing is presented as good practice, not a legal guarantee.
[REGION] Copyright and trademark rules for AI-assisted work differ by country and are still developing; the script gives no legal conclusion and says trademark checks are still needed before launch.
[VERSION] The concept images on the slides come from Google Gemini (DECISIONS.md; backup Adobe Firefly). Check its commercial-use terms before using the images in the video.

Every logo concept shown must be generated fresh from the concept-and-form prompt in content.md. Do not show, name or imitate any existing coffee brand or logo, and check the shown concepts with a reverse image search before recording.
Selam Tesfaye and the coffee roaster are fictional; roastery stock footage must not show real packaging, brand names or logos.
L08 is not a screen-demo lesson: the Figma redraw steps are shown as slides built from screenshots.

Hook.voiceover: An image generator gives you a logo that looks finished. Clean edges, nice colours and a clever shape. So why would a professional designer still redraw it from the beginning?

Explain.voiceover: Last time, we built moodboards. Now we move to the mark itself. This lesson is about logo exploration, with AI as a sketchbook, not final art.

slide.title: Logo Exploration: AI as Sketchbook, Not Final Art
slide.body: AI for Brand and Product Design · Lesson 8 of 14

Explain.voiceover: Image generators are useful early in logo design, when you explore many shapes, metaphors and compositions. Prompt with the idea and the form, not with existing logos. For example, a coffee bean that is also a sun rising over hills. Simple flat vector symbol, two colours, thick even lines, no text.

slide.title: Prompt with concept and form
slide.body: Concept: 'a coffee bean that is also a sun rising over hills' · Form: 'simple flat vector symbol, two colours, thick even lines, no text, white background'

Explain.voiceover: Change one variable at a time. Geometric or organic. Open or closed. Symmetric or not. Then choose a direction based on the brief, not on which image looks most polished.
Explain.on_screen_text: Choose by the brief, not the polish.

Explain.voiceover: But raw AI logos carry three risks. The first is similarity. Generators learn from huge image collections that include many logos, so a result can look close to an existing mark without you knowing. Use a reverse image search, and remember that official trademark checks are still needed before launch.

slide.title: Risk 1: Similarity
slide.body: Trained on huge image collections, including logos · May look close to an existing mark · Reverse image search helps · Official trademark checks still needed

Explain.voiceover: The second risk is weak scalability. Generated images are pixels, not vectors. Edges are uneven, details disappear at small sizes, and shapes do not follow a grid. A logo must work as a tiny browser icon, and on the side of a building.

slide.title: Risk 2: Scalability
slide.body: Left: pixel logo zoomed in, uneven edges, details lost at 16 px. Right: vector logo, crisp at 16 px and on a building wall.

Explain.voiceover: The third risk is ownership. Copyright rules for work made mostly by AI are still unclear, and they differ by country. If the client cannot own their logo, a competitor might be able to use something very similar.

slide.title: Risk 3: Ownership
slide.body: Copyright for mostly AI-made work is unclear and differs by country. If the client cannot own it, others may use something very similar.

Explain.voiceover: So, redraw. Choose the direction, then rebuild it yourself in Figma as a clean vector. Use a grid, make your own decisions about proportions, curves and weight, and simplify until it works small. That is better design, and clearly your own work. But it is good practice, not a legal guarantee.

slide.title: The redraw practice
slide.body: AI concept → grid in Figma → your proportions, curves, weight → simplify for small sizes → clean vector. Footer: good practice, not a legal guarantee

Explain.voiceover: Think of an AI concept as a photo reference for a painter. The photo helps you see the idea, but the painting comes from your own decisions with the brush. Copying the photo line by line is tracing. Interpreting it is design.
Explain.stock_query: painter working from photo reference at easel

Demonstrate.voiceover: Let's see this in practice. Selam Tesfaye is a brand designer in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia. Her client is a small coffee roaster that sells to cafés. The brief asks for a mark that suggests origin, warmth and care.

She generates ten concepts with prompts like this one: a coffee cherry combined with a rising sun, as a simple flat symbol, with no text. She puts the ten in Figma and scores each against the brief. Meaning, simplicity, and difference from typical coffee logos.

slide.title: Ten concepts, scored
slide.body: Prompt strip: 'simple flat vector symbol, a coffee cherry combined with a rising sun, two colours, thick even lines, no text, white background.' Below: a grid of 10 generated concepts in Figma, each with scores for meaning, simplicity and difference.

Demonstrate.voiceover: She picks a direction where the sun's rays become the lines of a coffee bean. A reverse image search finds no close matches. But she writes a note: visual search is not a trademark clearance.

slide.title: The chosen direction
slide.body: Concept: the sun's rays become the lines of a coffee bean. Sticky note: 'Visual search is not a trademark clearance.'

Demonstrate.voiceover: Then she redraws the mark in Figma. She sets up a forty-eight unit grid, and draws the bean with the ellipse and pen tools. She makes the rays equal width, with equal gaps. One ray disappears at sixteen pixels, so she removes it.

slide.title: Redrawing in Figma
slide.body: Screenshot sequence: 48-unit grid → bean drawn with Ellipse and Pen tools → rays of equal width and gaps → one ray removed because it vanishes at 16 px

Demonstrate.voiceover: She converts the outlines into one clean vector shape, and tests it at sixteen, sixty-four and five hundred and twelve pixels. Her file notes that the concept was explored with an image generator, the final mark was redrawn by hand, and a trademark search and ownership advice are recommended before launch.

slide.title: Tested at three sizes
slide.body: The final mark at 16 px, 64 px and 512 px. File note: 'Concept explored with an image generator; final mark redrawn by hand. Trademark search and ownership advice recommended before launch.'

Demonstrate.voiceover: A common mistake is to auto-trace an AI image and call it redrawn. That keeps the uneven shapes, and adds no real design decisions. Another mistake is believing that redrawing makes a logo legally safe. It does not. Ownership and similarity still need proper checks.

Recap.voiceover: Let's recap. First, use image generators as a sketchbook for fast logo exploration, prompting with concept and form, not existing logos. Second, raw AI logos are risky. They may look like existing marks, they scale poorly, and their copyright protection is uncertain. Third, redraw your chosen direction by hand in Figma, and still recommend trademark and legal checks.

slide.title: Key takeaways
slide.body: 1. AI = sketchbook: prompt with concept and form. 2. Raw AI logos: similarity, scalability, ownership risks. 3. Redraw by hand; still recommend trademark and legal checks.

CTA.voiceover: Now it is your turn. In the exercise below this video, you will generate ten logo concepts, pick one direction, and redraw it as a vector mark in Figma at three sizes. It takes about forty minutes. In the next lesson, we build colour, type and accessible brand systems. See you there.
